loci.name: n6-residual-scoping-legitimate-or-gerrymandered
loci.one_line: Is N6's four-conjunct residual (crossed x surrogate-class x optimizer x two-way decomposition, offline) a load-bearing scoping or a circle drawn around the answer to dodge RaM Table 3 and DiBO Table 2?
loci.rationale: This is the existential item and the contradiction graph already rates it high relevance (cluster n6-residual-width). The width sweep found RaM (Tan et al., ICLR 2025, note 241011502) contains a genuine 9x2 crossed grid (Table 3, 'Versatility of ranking loss') inside a paper the submission already cites for the OPPOSITE characterization ('surrogate-class comparisons hold the optimizer constant'), and three prior vault fetches of the same paper never surfaced Table 3 -- a concrete demonstration that the prior audit's verdicts needed re-checking, not trusting. DiBO (note 260317919) adds a second 2026 near-miss (backbone x training-stage, 2x3, descriptive). The residual is currently defended on three grounds (loss-type != model-class, bundled-methods != optimizer-factor, descriptive != decomposed) but none of the three is yet written into the paper, and a hostile reviewer from Tan et al.'s own group is a live audience. Depth investigation should (a) independently stress-test whether the three grounds actually hold once stated formally -- is 'nine bundled methods' really disqualifying if three of the nine (BO-qEI, CMA-ES, Grad. Ascent) ARE clean optimizer settings under one shared surrogate-loss factor, i.e. does a 3x2 sub-grid survive inside RaM's own Table 3 that is closer to a kill than the full 9x2 reading suggests -- and (b) run one more fresh sweep (2026 AutoML/NAS fANOVA literature, drug-discovery/materials black-box optimization adjacent fields) since the near-miss list has grown twice already in this same audit and an existential claim deserves a second independent pass, not just the first one's confidence.

opposing_positions.position: Unowned: no prior work runs a crossed surrogate x optimizer factorial with a two-way variance decomposition in offline MBO. RaM Table 3 and DiBO Table 2 are near-misses, not instances, because loss-type is not model-class, the nine RaM entries are bundled methods not a clean optimizer factor, and both report descriptively with zero ANOVA/variance-decomposition language.

RaM Table 3 is a genuine 9x2 crossed grid in offline MBO inside a paper the submission cites and mischaracterizes as optimizer-constant; a sub-grid of RaM's own nine entries (BO-qEI, CMA-ES, Grad. Ascent are clean numerical search routines, not generative/inverse-modelling methods like CbAS/MINs/PGS) may already satisfy the 'optimizer factor' half of N6's residual, narrowing the fourth conjunct (two-way decomposition) to the only ground left standing.

loci.name: buried-interaction-effect-methodological-grounding
loci.one_line: Is there an authoritative factorial-design/ANOVA-methodology citation -- beyond Moosbauer's negative framing -- for 'a significant, stable surrogate x optimizer interaction is the specific payoff a crossed design buys over OFAT,' and does that literature require a simple-effects decomposition before the interaction can be safely promoted to the abstract?
loci.rationale: The orchestrator's own artifact-level check (results/bootstrap_eta_corners.json, reported in research/temp/findings-so-far.md's starred section) found eta^2_inter = 0.146-0.165 in all four engine corners, bootstrap CIs excluding zero in every one, and it is the MOST stable effect in the paper (range 0.018 vs the headline surrogate effect's range 0.167) -- yet 'interaction' appears exactly once in main.tex, only as Moosbauer's stated reason for declining OFAT, never as the paper's own result. This is tagged FOLD-INTO-THIS-PAPER/CHEAP and ranked first in deliverable (iii) already, but the only citation available to justify why the interaction matters is Moosbauer's negative one (a paper that names fANOVA and declines the two-way analysis) -- the paper has no positive citation for 'a significant interaction is definitionally the thing OFAT designs cannot estimate.' The corpus's own Moosbauer note (already fetched, ar5iv full text) states this only defensively. A depth investigation should chase the classical factorial-design methodology this traces to (Fisher's original interaction-effects rationale, or a modern methods reference such as Montgomery's Design and Analysis of Experiments, or an ML-specific paper on interaction effects in benchmark ANOVAs) to give the promoted claim an affirmative rather than a borrowed-negative citation, and should separately check whether that same methodology literature requires a simple-effects decomposition (which specific surrogate-optimizer pairing drives the interaction) before a significant omnibus interaction can be responsibly interpreted -- the paper has never computed this decomposition, and 'we found an interaction and did not decompose it' is exactly the kind of incompleteness an ANOVA-literate reviewer would flag if the interaction is promoted to the abstract as this audit recommends.

simple effects decomposition significant interaction small sample ANOVA guidance

loci.name: ntk-width-citations-unverified-and-mechanism-tension
loci.one_line: Jacot (NTK), Lee (DNN-as-GP), Lee (wide-nets-evolve-as-linear-models), and Rahaman (spectral bias) motivate Elimination 2's width ablation and are never fetched anywhere in this re-audit -- and does citing Xu et al.'s asymptotic NTK linear-extrapolation theorem as the paper's top recommended positive mechanism (deliverable iii) sit in tension with the paper's own finding that the gap does not change across a 10.7x width sweep?
loci.rationale: I confirmed by direct search of the vault (zero hits for jacot/lee2018/lee2019/rahaman/spectral-bias/NTK/neural-tangent across every note in the corpus) and by grepping research/temp/coverage-gaps.md, coverage-matrix.md, search-plan.md, and redundancy-audit.md (zero mentions in all four) that these four citations -- which main.tex's Elimination 2 uses to motivate the entire width ablation ('wide networks approach GP behaviour [Jacot/Lee/Lee]; finite networks show spectral bias [Rahaman]') -- have never been fetched or grepped in this audit, unlike essentially every other load-bearing citation (SNGP, Fan, Shahriari, Demsar, Melis, L/R/W, Abe, dewolf2022intervals, ghasemipour2022pessimistic all got full-text verification per findings-so-far.md). docs/CLAIM_LEDGER.md's D13 row additionally asserts an unverified numeric threshold -- 'width 96 << n>=512 agreement range' -- attributed to Lee et al. 2019, that appears nowhere in the current re-audit's verified findings and traces only to the prior (not-yet-re-checked) NOVELTY_V3 pass. Separately, and more substantively: the width ablation's whole rhetorical structure is 'wide networks are asymptotically GP-like (NTK theory), so if the gap were an under-parameterization artifact it should shrink with width -- it does not, so width is eliminated.' But deliverable (iii)'s top-ranked candidate positive mechanism is Xu et al.'s NTK-regime linear-extrapolation theorem (note 200911848, already fetched and verified), which is explicitly an asymptotic, width-dependent convergence result. If the paper folds in Xu et al. as its positive mechanism while ALSO having eliminated width as a factor, it must reconcile why a width-dependent theorem explains a width-independent empirical finding -- most likely by arguing the operative fact is piecewise-linear extrapolation (a property of ANY finite ReLU network, independent of the NTK limit), which is a different and more elementary citation than Xu et al.'s asymptotic result. This reconciliation is currently absent and a depth investigator should determine which citation (Xu et al.'s asymptotic theorem, or a finite-width piecewise-linearity result such as the ReLU-far-field-overconfidence literature) actually applies to the paper's real architecture (2-hidden-layer, width 96-1024, 35 epochs, Adam, not NTK-parameterized).

loci.name: eta-squared-bias-primary-source-verification
loci.one_line: Are Kelley (1935) and Olejnik & Algina (2003) -- the two primary sources for 'eta-squared is positively biased at small n, omega-squared/epsilon-squared are the bias-corrected alternatives' -- reachable directly, or is there a citable, accessible alternative primary that supports the same recommendation Mandatory Fix 9 rests on secondhand?
loci.rationale: research/temp/coverage-gaps.md explicitly records this as one of only three genuine remaining gaps after wave 1: 'Kelley (1935) and Olejnik & Algina (2003) -- verified only secondhand... Both are paywalled (APA/JMLR/ResearchGate/academia.edu all blocked). The empirical half is first-hand and decisive; the citation half is secondhand.' This bears directly on Mandatory Fix 9 (research/temp/findings-so-far.md), one of the cheapest, cleanest wins in the whole audit -- the paper's own bootstrap artifacts already show eta^2 is upward-biased in all four corners (+0.0099 to +0.0184) and bias-correcting makes the headline claim STRONGER (0.351->0.395 vs the reported 0.367->0.405), but the citation for WHY omega^2/epsilon^2 are the standard bias-corrected alternatives currently rests only on the JOSS `effectsize` package documentation quoting Kelley and Olejnik & Algina, not on either primary directly. A depth investigator with broader access (institutional proxy, Google Books preview, a citing paper that reproduces Kelley's or Olejnik & Algina's exact bias formula, or a widely-available methods textbook such as Maxwell & Delaney's Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data) could either confirm the primaries firsthand or identify a citable, accessible substitute -- converting the one remaining secondhand link in an otherwise fully first-hand-verified fix.

Olejnik Algina 2003 generalized eta squared omega squared bias correction
